title: BOOK FOUR / CHAPTER ONE. On the principles of human salvation, namely the grace of paternal mercy
english: BOOK FOUR. On the principles and means of human salvation.
CHAPTER ONE. On the principles of human salvation, and namely on the grace of paternal mercy.

Up to this point, in three books we have treated the nature and constitution of sacred theology; then the last and absolutely highest end of the human being — namely the supernatural blessedness of soul and body; and finally (1) the humans creation, by which God made him fit to attain this highest end, endowed with righteousness and innocence, so that after living a pleasant and quiet life in sincere and constant love and worship of the Creator without hardships he might be transferred, immortal and without sense of death, into heavenly, eternal, and absolutely blessed life; and (2) his defection, when by Satans persuasion and impulse and by his own imprudence he lost the blessedness to which he had been divinely ordered, and offended his Creator by wicked disobedience, so that he became heir not of eternal life but of eternal death, and as one guilty of divine majesty lese-majeste, stripped of those gifts received above his natures condition, cannot by himself see, find, and keep that way which leads to the blessedness destined for him at the beginning.

I. There follow now the principles on which eternal salvation depends; and they are nothing other than acts of divine grace, by which Gods mercy and justice are so tempered that the sinful human can escape Gods wrath and damnation and regain Gods friendship and eternal life.

title: II. Three principles of salvation; grace as free favor, not infused habit
english: II. The principles of human salvation are the grace of paternal mercy, of fraternal redemption, and of Gods heavenly calling.

Since our salvation and Gods friendship are wholly desperate whether we turn to ourselves or to all or any other creatures — because Gods justice, whose precept we violated, cannot otherwise be satisfied — the first principle of this friendship and of our salvation is truly Gods grace. By this we do not mean that general beneficence of God by which all created things are conserved and governed; for that would stand even if the human had never been received into grace. We mean rather the acts of divine benevolence and philanthropy by which God pitied the fallen human race when He saw it wholly sunk in eternal ruin and unable to be freed from it unless He Himself came to its aid (Ephesians 1:5; 2:4; Titus 3:4).

First, therefore, when the divine writings say we have been saved by grace, by grace is to be understood nothing but Gods mercy and free favor toward us. And so the Papists sense must be rejected, who here interpret grace as an infused quality or habit — whether the habit of charity or another distinct from charity. This grace itself was given us in Christ before the ages of the world (2 Timothy 1:9). Nor is it to be doubted that God foresaw the humans fall before all times, even though it happened in time, and so foresaw the miseries and punishments in which the human race was to be entangled; and second, that just as God pitied humans in time, so by the very foresight of those miseries He pitied from eternity and decreed when He would help.

Yet since God is not only good but also just and constant in His words, it cannot be that He fail to exact the severest punishment for sins, and what He Himself pronounced must most certainly be fulfilled: in whatever day you eat the forbidden fruit, you shall die the death. Therefore it is most necessary to hold that Gods decree to free humans was made according to His mercy in such a way that His truth and justice were in no way violated. From this we gather that the principle of our salvation is truly an admirable tempering of divine mercy and justice, unsearchable to human reason — so that justice is satisfied, and yet mercy also has its place to help the wretched.

title: III–V. Paternal mercy as first principle; object is the whole human race as miserable and stained by sin
english: III. The grace of paternal MERCY is the first principle of human salvation, by which God so embraces the whole human race that He wills all humans to be saved, and according to His wisdom and justice orders and determines for them the amplest means of salvation. The proper seats of this first principle are Genesis 3:8,15; John 3:16; 1 Timothy 2:4; Titus 2:11; 2 Peter 3:9.

IV. Here its object and mode are to be considered. V. The object of the grace of mercy is the whole human race, as miserable and stained by sin. Our Savior teaches this by the word world in John 3:16. For it is certain that world here does not mean the whole system of heaven and earth with all its inhabitants produced from nothing by God, but only the human race. In the sacred writings this word sometimes signifies the human race universally, sometimes a certain part of it — either only believers gathered from the whole world into Gods kingdom, or only the impious condemned from the whole world.

It is also plain that world here is not taken in that last sense of John 17:9 and 14:17. Nor does Christ here mean by world only the elect as already separated from the world, but the whole human race taken universally, as by nature it lies in sin, and as it is commonly called through the gospel to repentance and faith in Christ (Mark 16:15; 1 John 2:2). Yet although God so loved the whole world universally, this love peculiarly and chiefly regards believers.

We distinguish three post-fall states of the human: first, of nature or common corruption; second, of grace or regeneration; third, of impenitence or final hardening, where at last Gods love stops and sheer wrath and judgment overflow upon the obstinate.

title: VI. From the object: love of all and of some; no clash with election
english: VI. From what we have said about the object of the divine grace of mercy, two things especially become plain.

First is the great controversy whether God so loved all humans, or only some. Who will deny that God singularly loved believers, whom He also elected and acknowledged from eternity, above all other humans? Who will affirm that God so loves unbelievers who remain without repentance in their unbelief, once He has already judged and condemned them? Who on the other side will assert that God in no way loved those to whom He so often, variously, seriously, and from the heart offers His love and grace — and against whom He is so vehemently angry, judging and condemning them precisely because they do not believe in the Son and spurn and reject love and grace?

Second: this love of God that embraces the whole world does not clash with the election of Gods children, and it by no means follows that if God so loved the whole world He therefore also elected the whole to salvation. Here the Saviors sayings in John 15:19; 13:18; Matthew 22:14 have place. For election first distinguishes the children of God, whom He gifts with salvation by His grace, from the remaining world that by its own fault remains in unbelief.

title: VII–IX. Mode of mercy: amplitude in gift, demand, and promise
english: VII. The mode of the grace of mercy consists in its amplitude and determination. VIII. Its amplitude is set in the gift, in what is demanded, and in the promise.

IX. First, Gods overflowing love toward us is made plain by the gift. For He did not love us because of any merit of ours, as if we had first given Him something He should repay (Romans 11:35), or because we loved Him first (1 John 4:19), but much more because when we had deserved sheer wrath and indignation, and had as far as in us lay destroyed the image we had received from Him at the beginning — yes, and overturned what we owed Him, fear, honor, love, obedience, even our soul and body — when from servants we had become enemies, and when He could have given us the wages of sins, death and hell: He gave us the image of His substance, His only-begotten Son. It was grace to Israel to be given the servant Moses and David: how much greater the grace that we are given not a servant but the Son of God, and Him only-begotten — and not merely as prophet and teacher of salvation, as the Socinians invent, or as an earthly savior, as the Jews, but as eternal Savior, High Priest, and King, who offered Himself as a true propitiatory sacrifice unto death for us, not to lead us from Egypt into Canaan but from death and hell into heaven.

Second, the grace of divine mercy is plain from what He demands of us. For God does not exact Levitical sacrifices and gifts, nor servile and forced obedience to the Mosaic law, but the filial obedience of faith — and He demands this in such a way that He also wills to work it in us by His Spirit.
Third, and most of all, it shines from the promise made to us in the Son of God: that all who believe in Him should not perish but have eternal life.

title: Determination of mercy: only in the Son; by repentance and faith; by the light of Word and Spirit
english: The determination of the grace of mercy is that by which God, through His wisdom and justice, so limits, measures, and orders it that He receives the sinful human into His friendship, absolves from sin, and gifts with eternal life — not without Christ His Son or outside Him, nor without repentance and faith, but by requiring this in accordance with His justice and promising life through Christough Christ, and by grace bestowing both.

Three things therefore restrain and limit the universal philanthropy by divine wisdom and justice. First: God loved the world stained by sin, yet not so as to love it without the Son or outside the Son, or to remit sins and bless it without satisfaction and expiation, but only in the Son and through the Son, whom He gave as mediator and propitiator.
Second: after God gave His Son for reconciliation, He so loved the world in Him and reconciled it to Himself through Him that remission of sins is not obtained without repentance and faith.

Third: by the force of that new covenant of grace in Christ God so loved the world that He not only, according to His justice, exacted obedience and promised life as in the old covenant of the law, but also by His grace wills to work and bestow both what the gospel demands — the obedience of faith — and what it promises — the most certain consolation of remission of all sins and of eternal life; yet not by bare omnipotence and mere miracles, or by forcing humans as it were violently to faith, but by the light of Word and Spirit in the gospel.

title: Corollaries: unequal light of grace; election mystery; decree ordered to Christs merit and means
english: From what has been said the following corollaries flow.

1. It does not clash with the universal grace and philanthropy by which God loved the world, nor with Christs merit, that God grants one people or region greater light — and so also greater grace and love — than others, and more or less according to the diversity of ages and times.
2. Nor does it clash with Gods love and Christs merit that even at the same time and place He grants one human greater light and grace than another, each according to the measure of Christs gifts.

3. In this disposition of God — when, where, and how He lets the light and efficacy of His Word and Spirit shine and work in the world — consists properly the highest mystery of the election of Gods children. For according to His counsel and purpose God from eternity mercifully appointed to dispense to fallen humans in Christ this free light of Word and Spirit.

4. Even though God was moved not by foresight of works or of faith or of any other animal condition in sinful humans, but by His alone unmerited mercy, to elect some of them to life: still this decree of election cannot simply be called absolute; for although on the animals side in the human there is no determination or condition of it, yet there is some on Gods side, who Himself bound it to Christs merit and to the means — namely the preaching of the gospel and the faith that applies it.

title: Cause of damnation in humans themselves; Cap.1 close toward Cap.2 on the grace of redemption
english: Reprobation is the just sentence of Gods judgment upon all impenitent unbelievers. First, the fault is not the Fathers. For He sent His Son into this world not to judge it but to save it. By right, according to the rigor of His justice, He could have sent His Son to judge and condemn the world for sins against the law, because the whole lies in evil: yet from sheer grace He first sent Him not for judgment.

The proximate and chief cause of damnation is in humans themselves. The Lord does not speak simply of habitual and innate unbelief, but of actual, affected, obstinate unbelief joined with perpetual impenitence. This is the head of all sins, which God by His justice and truth cannot but condemn. The reason is that they do not believe in the name of the only-begotten Son of God: outside which name there is no salvation.

From all this it is plain that love of darkness and hatred of light — the proper cause of humans judgment and damnation — is to be sought only in themselves. See the excellent theologian Dr. Johann Bergius in his explanation of the saying So God loved the world, on the causes of human salvation and damnation, published at Berlin in 1629.
CHAPTER TWO follows, on the grace of redemption.
